description: Mental rehearsal, imagery and arousal control techniques that prepare athletes for competition.
content_html:
The Psychology of Preparation

Elite sport is won and lost in the mind as well as the body. A physically fit athlete who is mentally unprepared — distracted, under-aroused or paralysed by anxiety — will underperform against a technically inferior opponent who is perfectly prepared. The spec covers mental preparation strategies that athletes use to optimise their psychological state before and during competition: these include warm-up, mental rehearsal and the management of arousal.

The Physical Warm-Up as Mental Preparation

The physical warm-up is more than a physiological necessity. It also serves as a structured routine that transitions the athlete psychologically from a resting state into competitive readiness. A familiar warm-up routine cues the brain to prepare for performance, narrowing attentional focus, reducing distraction and helping the athlete reach the correct mental state. This is why elite athletes — from Dina Asher-Smith to Andy Murray — follow consistent pre-competition routines. The predictability of the routine is psychologically calming; it signals to the brain that this moment is no different from the many successful training sessions that preceded it.

Mental Rehearsal

Mental rehearsal is the deliberate mental practice of a performance. The athlete imagines performing the skill or executing the competition plan in precise detail, activating the same neural pathways as actual physical execution. Research in sport psychology consistently shows that mental rehearsal combined with physical practice produces better outcomes than physical practice alone, because it reinforces the motor programme, builds confidence and allows the athlete to mentally “experience” success before the competition.

Mental rehearsal is often used alongside imagery. Where mental rehearsal is the broader cognitive activity (practising a performance mentally), imagery specifically involves the richness of the sensory experience: the feel of the surface underfoot, the sound of the crowd, the weight of the javelin in the hand, the visual perspective as the ball approaches. Well-practised imagery is almost indistinguishable in the brain from actual experience, which is why it is such a powerful preparation tool.

There are two perspectives athletes use in imagery. Internal imagery (first-person: seeing through your own eyes as if performing) is most effective for skill execution and kinaesthetic feel. External imagery (third-person: watching yourself perform from the outside, like watching a video) is more effective for analysing technical errors or visualising positional and tactical aspects of performance. Many athletes combine both.

Key Fact

Mental rehearsal is the cognitive simulation of a performance or skill without physical execution. Imagery is a specific form of mental rehearsal that incorporates rich sensory detail (sights, sounds, feel, emotions). Together they reinforce motor programmes, build confidence and help athletes manage arousal before competition.

Arousal and Its Effects

Arousal is the level of mental and physical activation an athlete experiences. It is not the same as anxiety, though the two are related. Arousal describes a continuum from complete relaxation (e.g. deep sleep) through to extreme activation (e.g. panic). Every sport task has an optimal arousal level that produces the best performance. A dart thrower needs low-moderate arousal for fine motor control; a rugby player charging into a tackle needs high arousal for explosive power. The challenge of mental preparation is reaching the correct arousal level for the specific task — not too high, not too low.

Anxiety is the negative, uncontrolled end of the arousal spectrum. Somatic anxiety refers to the physical symptoms: racing heart, sweating, muscle tension, nausea. Cognitive anxiety refers to the mental symptoms: negative self-talk, inability to concentrate, catastrophic thinking. Both forms impair performance if they are not managed.

Techniques for Managing Arousal

Several techniques are used to raise or lower arousal levels to meet the demands of the task. To raise arousal (for under-aroused athletes in low-stimulation situations), coaches use energising music, pre-game team talks with vivid imagery, positive self-talk and physical activation warm-ups. To lower arousal (for over-aroused athletes experiencing anxiety), specific relaxation techniques are used.

Deep breathing (controlled breathing) is the simplest and most widely used arousal-reduction technique. By deliberately slowing the breath — typically inhaling for four counts and exhaling for six — the athlete activates the parasympathetic nervous system, counteracting the adrenaline-driven “fight or flight” response. A penalty-taker in football who pauses before their run-up, breathes deeply and exhales slowly is using controlled breathing to lower their arousal to an optimal level for precise motor execution.

Progressive muscle relaxation involves systematically tensing then releasing each major muscle group, starting from the feet and working upward. By experiencing the contrast between tension and relaxation, the athlete learns to recognise and release unwanted muscle tension. This directly addresses somatic anxiety — the physical tightness that impairs fluid movement.

Positive self-talk involves deliberately replacing negative internal dialogue (“I’m going to mess this up”) with constructive, affirming statements (“I have practised this hundreds of times and I am ready”). It counteracts cognitive anxiety by redirecting attentional focus from failure to process. A swimmer who replaces “what if I false-start” with “react to the gun, drive off the block” is using positive self-talk as an attentional control tool.

A pre-performance routine is a fixed sequence of physical and mental actions completed before executing a skill or competing. Golfers go through the same address routine before every shot; basketball players bounce the ball a set number of times before a free throw; gymnasts perform the same mental walkthrough before mounting the beam. The consistency of the routine serves several functions: it narrows attentional focus to task-relevant cues, it raises arousal to the optimal level for that specific skill, it triggers the mental state associated with successful past performances, and it reduces the impact of distracting environmental factors (crowd noise, opponent’s behaviour). On exam questions about mental preparation, mentioning the pre-performance routine and explaining its psychological mechanism (attentional control, arousal calibration) earns additional marks.

Students often assume that more arousal always means better performance — that a very excited, highly motivated athlete will always outperform a calm one. This is not the case. For tasks requiring fine motor control, decision-making under pressure or sustained technical precision (a golf putt, a snooker break, a gymnastic beam routine), excessive arousal causes tremor, loss of coordination and poor decision-making. The optimal arousal level for fine motor tasks is significantly lower than for gross motor tasks like a sprint start or a rugby tackle. Over-arousal is a genuine performance hazard. This is why mental preparation focuses on reaching the RIGHT level of arousal, not the highest level.

Key Fact

Arousal-reduction techniques: deep breathing (activates parasympathetic nervous system, slows heart rate), progressive muscle relaxation (releases somatic tension by systematically contracting then releasing muscle groups), positive self-talk (redirects attention from anxiety-generating thoughts to process cues). All three can be used in the minutes before competition.
exam_tip_html: For questions about mental rehearsal, explain what it is (mentally simulating a performance in detail), why it works (reinforces motor programmes, builds confidence) and how it is used by an athlete (e.g. a high diver mentally performing their routine in detail before mounting the board). A common error is to describe mental rehearsal as simply “thinking about the sport” — that is not specific enough. For arousal questions, remember that the goal is optimal arousal, not maximum arousal. Name the technique, explain the mechanism (not just the outcome), and apply it to the specific sport in the question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mental rehearsal involves cognitively simulating a performance without physical execution; imagery adds rich sensory detail. Both reinforce motor programmes and build pre-competition confidence by allowing the athlete to mentally experience success.
  • Arousal is a continuum of activation from sleep to extreme excitement. Each sport task has an optimal arousal level — fine motor skills require lower arousal, gross motor tasks higher. Over-arousal causes anxiety and impairs performance.
  • Techniques for controlling arousal: deep breathing and progressive muscle relaxation lower arousal by activating the parasympathetic nervous system and releasing muscle tension. Positive self-talk and pre-performance routines help maintain attentional focus and reach the optimal mental state.

practice_questions.text: Identify one technique an athlete can use to lower their arousal before competing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: deep breathing / controlled breathing / progressive muscle relaxation / positive self-talk / mental rehearsal / imagery (accept any valid arousal-reduction technique named without explanation).

practice_questions.text: Define 'mental rehearsal' and give one example of how a gymnast might use it before a competition.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly defining mental rehearsal: a cognitive technique in which the athlete mentally simulates a performance or skill in detail without physically executing it. 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. a gymnast mentally walks through their floor routine, visualising each element in sequence, including the timing, the feel of each movement and a successful landing, in the warm-up area before their turn).

practice_questions.text: Explain how deep breathing helps a performer reduce anxiety before competing.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that deep breathing involves deliberately slowing and deepening the breath; 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (slow, deep breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system, counteracting the adrenaline-driven stress response and lowering heart rate and muscle tension); 1 mark for applying to a sporting example (e.g. a penalty-taker who takes two slow, deep breaths before their run-up is lowering their arousal to the level needed for the precise motor control that penalty-taking requires).

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level archer experiences high anxiety before competitions, leading to trembling and loss of concentration. Discuss two mental preparation strategies her coach could recommend.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for naming two valid strategies (e.g. progressive muscle relaxation + positive self-talk). 1 mark each for explaining how each strategy addresses the specific problem described. Acceptable content: progressive muscle relaxation — systematically tensing and releasing muscle groups releases the somatic tension that causes trembling; the archer practises this in the warm-up area before competing; positive self-talk — replaces the negative internal dialogue ('I will miss') with process-focused cues ('breathe, anchor, release') that redirect attention from anxiety to technique, addressing the concentration loss.

practice_questions.text: A club-level sprinter uses mental rehearsal as part of her pre-competition warm-up. Analyse how mental rehearsal can improve her performance at a county athletics meeting.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mental rehearsal clearly defined; mechanisms explained (motor programme reinforcement, confidence building, arousal regulation, attentional control); consistently applied to sprinting performance; both the psychological and potential physiological mechanisms considered; technically accurate language.

Secure: Mental rehearsal defined; at least two mechanisms explained; mostly applied to sprinting; generally accurate.

Developing: Mental rehearsal described; one or two mechanisms mentioned; limited analysis of how it specifically improves sprinting performance.

Emerging: Basic description of mental rehearsal with little analysis.

Acceptable content: reinforces the motor programme for the sprint start without physical fatigue; builds confidence by mentally experiencing a successful start and race; helps regulate arousal to the high level required for a sprint without tipping into over-arousal; narrows attentional focus to the start signal and drive phase; the sprinter arrives at the blocks having already “run” the race successfully in her mind, reducing the novelty and unpredictability of the competition environment.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which mental preparation strategies can improve sporting performance, considering evidence both for and against their effectiveness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of mental preparation strategies (mental rehearsal, imagery, arousal management, pre-performance routines); evidence of effectiveness discussed; limitations acknowledged (strategies require practice to be effective; novices may lack the kinaesthetic experience to make imagery meaningful; high anxiety may overwhelm technique-based strategies; other factors such as physical fitness and tactical knowledge also determine performance); consistent sporting examples; balanced, justified conclusion.

Secure: At least two strategies discussed with evidence of effectiveness; some limitations present; sporting examples used; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly benefits described; limited limitations; some sporting examples; argument largely one-sided.

Emerging: Basic description of mental preparation with little evaluative content.

For effectiveness: mental rehearsal + physical practice produces better outcomes than physical practice alone; arousal management enables performers to reach optimal states for specific tasks; pre-performance routines shown to stabilise performance under pressure; widely used by elite performers (consistent, structured routines before major events).

Against: strategies require long practice to work; novices may be unable to create meaningful imagery because they lack the kinaesthetic experience; no strategy eliminates the physical and tactical factors that also determine outcome; under extreme competition pressure, even well-practised routines can break down; not equally effective for all performers or all sports. Conclusion: mental preparation is an evidence-supported and important component of performance, particularly at elite level, but it is most effective as part of a comprehensive preparation that includes physical training, tactical knowledge and competition experience.

What is the key difference between mental rehearsal and imagery?
options: Mental rehearsal involves physical movement; imagery does not
Imagery incorporates rich sensory detail; mental rehearsal is broader cognitive simulation
Imagery is only used by beginners; mental rehearsal is for advanced performers
They are identical techniques with different names

right: Systematically releases physical muscle tension through contract-and-release cycles
Activates the parasympathetic nervous system to slow heart rate

glossary_terms.definition: A cognitive technique in which the athlete mentally simulates a performance or skill, visualising the movement in detail without physically executing it.
A form of mental rehearsal in which the athlete creates detailed sensory images of a performance, including sights, sounds, bodily sensations and emotions.
A general state of physiological and psychological activation that ranges from deep sleep to extreme excitement, and that affects an athlete's readiness to perform.
A negative emotional state characterised by feelings of worry, nervousness and apprehension, associated with high and uncontrolled arousal.
A controlled breathing technique in which the athlete slows and deepens their breathing to reduce physiological arousal and calm the body's stress response.
A relaxation technique in which the athlete progressively tenses and then relaxes each muscle group in turn to release physical tension caused by somatic anxiety.
